title: Rooted Water Collectives in a Modernist and Neoliberal Imaginary: Threats and Perspectives for Rural Water Commons
rationale: Full-text empirical qualitative comparative case study and action research paper examining household and community domestic/multiple-use rural water supply across three user-managed schemes in South Africa and Switzerland. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it empirically analyzes provider ownership and statutory regulatory structures (cooperative/user ownership vs. municipal water service monopoly and tendering rules under South Africa's WSA 1997/MSA 2000 and Swiss spatial planning law), municipal discretion toward 'legal grey zone' CBO schemes, upfront contribution and membership-cap eligibility rules, municipal-volunteer accountability structures, and subsidy merger conditionalities, linking them directly to household connection, reliability/continuity, and exclusion outcomes. Qualitative socio-legal studies are included for mechanism synthesis even without quantitative effect estimates.

title: Water Infrastructure Always In-the-Making: Distributing Water and Authority through the Water Supply Network in Moamba, Mozambique
rationale: This qualitative ethnographic case study in Moamba, Mozambique meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type readings of Criterion 2. Beyond its broader sociotechnical tinkering framework, it empirically documents concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing household piped water access and continuity—including utility cost-recovery barriers to network extension, utility accommodation of an unauthorized user-installed pipeline paired with formal billing contracts yet contested pipe ownership during shutoffs/repairs, conditional user labor/material requirements for repairs, community-enforced upfront and late-comer connection fee rules (50 MT vs. 500 MT) that exclude poorer households from private connections, and operator discretion over rotational rationing schedules. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies with identifiable population, exposure, outcome, and design are included for the mechanism synthesis.

title: Public-Private Community Partnerships in Infrastructure for the Poor
rationale: This comparative qualitative study of 20 infrastructure partnership case studies in 10 Asian/Pacific countries (undertaken in 2001 with focus group discussions and interviews in low-income slums) meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. title: Price-cap regulation of private water services for small towns in Burkina Faso based on solar energy
rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the paper addresses drinking-water access in small towns in Burkina Faso (c1=yes) and discusses rule-type regulatory and tariff mechanisms including price-cap regulation, volumetric/connection tariff rules, and 10-year private affermage contracts (c2=yes under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 reading), it is a prospective policy-design ('action-research') and ex-ante deterministic financial simulation study for 2016-2030 rather than an empirical evaluation of water service access (c3=no). Stakeholder working groups agreed on normative target tariffs, phased 2016-2030 universal coverage targets (Table 2), demand forecasts (Table 3), and standard engineering unit-cost assumptions (Annex 2) to simulate operator operating profit margins and required public CAPEX under solar versus fossil-fuel pumping, and the proposed policy had not yet been enacted. Moreover, household access coverage, consumption, and target tariffs are exogenous model assumptions rather than empirically measured access outcomes (c4=no).

title: The elephant in the room: Informality in Tanzania’s rural waterscape
rationale: This full-text qualitative empirical case study in Hai and Siha districts, Tanzania satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Using semi-structured interviews (n = 20) and organizational fieldwork data, it examines how formal rule-type mechanisms governing rural drinking water access—including autonomous Water Trust legal structures under a Water Service Facility Trust, structured cost-recovery tariffs, metered billing, full-cost private connection fee rules, disconnection threats, and performance-appraisal sanctions—interact with informal enforcement sanctions (naming/shaming non-payers) and informal accommodation/cross-subsidy mechanisms (means-assessed church bill support with tap attendants, diaspora connection funding, and committee arrears payment to avert public tap disconnection) to shape household piped connections, public standpipe access, 24/7 continuity, and affordability. Qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis regardless of lacking quantitative effect sizes.

title: Barcelona's water supply, 1867-1967: the transition to a modern system
rationale: This archival urban-history case study examines the 1867-1967 transition of Barcelona's domestic drinking-water and sanitation systems using primary municipal and utility archival records and quantitative historical supply/consumption series. Although framed broadly around long-term infrastructural modernization, it substantively analyzes rule-type institutional and regulatory mechanisms directly governing household access under Criterion 2 (both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings): private utility monopoly ownership (SGAB) favoring affluent central districts and excluding peripheral working-class areas, upfront concession/piping costs, 1891 sewer/toilet ordinances, and tenement landlords' persistence with rent-bundled trickle-feed contracts rather than individual meters despite the 1925 Royal Decree Municipal Health Regulations.
